title: 1 Samuel 2:22–26
context: Old Eli hears of his sons’ sins and rebukes them, but they do not listen. The narrator links their refusal to the LORD’s purpose to judge them, while Samuel grows in favor with the LORD and with people.

verses.text: Now Eli was very old; and he heard all that his sons did to all Israel, and how that they slept with the women who served at the door of the Tent of Meeting.
verses.arminianNotes: Eli, very old, hears what his sons do, including sleeping with the women serving at the Tent of Meeting. Arminian readers see their sin extending to sexual immorality at the sanctuary.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the depth of the sons’ corruption. Women serving at the tent’s door are also mentioned in Exodus 38:8, which highlights how sacred space was defiled.

verses.text: He said to them, “Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people.
verses.arminianNotes: Eli asks, “Why do you do such things? For I hear of your evil dealings from all these people.” Arminian readers see a father finally rebuking his sons, though without firm action.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a mild rebuke that does not match the seriousness of the sin. The later judgment in 3:13 notes that Eli did not restrain them.

verses.text: No, my sons; for it is not a good report that I hear! You make the LORD’s people disobey.
verses.arminianNotes: Eli says, “No, my sons; for it is not a good report that I hear! You make the LORD’s people disobey.” Arminian readers see concern that the priests lead others into sin.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the wider damage caused by corrupt leaders. Their behavior harms not only themselves but the people entrusted to their care.

verses.text: If one man sins against another, God will judge him; but if a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?” Notwithstanding, they didn’t listen to the voice of their father, because the LORD intended to kill them.
verses.arminianNotes: Eli warns, “… if a man sins against the LORD, who will intercede for him?” Yet “they didn’t listen … because the LORD intended to kill them.” Arminian readers often see God confirming a judgment the sons had brought on themselves through persistent rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers often see God’s settled judicial purpose as an underlying reason for their refusal to listen, while insisting that the sons remained fully guilty. Many in this tradition read it alongside texts such as Exodus 9:12 and Romans 9:18.
verses.keyContrast: Arminian readers generally take “the LORD intended to kill them” as God’s judicial response to the sons’ long, freely chosen rebellion: their refusal was their own, and God confirmed the judgment they had invited. Reformed readers generally see God’s prior judicial decree as the deeper reason they would not listen, without making God the author of their sin or lessening their guilt. Both readings hold the sons fully accountable and God just in judging them; there is diversity within each tradition on how strongly the verse’s “because” should be pressed.

verses.text: The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with the LORD and also with men.
verses.arminianNotes: “The child Samuel grew on, and increased in favor both with the LORD and also with men.” Arminian readers see faithful growth that contrasts sharply with the sons’ rebellion.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s favor resting on Samuel. Luke 2:52 later uses similar language of Jesus, and many readers note the echo.
